Publisher full text from XML with section and paragraph locators (jats_text)

entry.evidence: The precursory activity we observe at Fagradalsfjall, however, involves both a decline in seismicity and deformation.

sequences.source_document: Sigmundsson et al. 2022, Nature 609, 523-528 (XML text and PDF)

steps.action: States the standard expectation, from Voight's material failure forecast method, that precursory strain and seismicity escalate towards eruption onset.
steps.quote: derived a method of interpreting escalating rates of observed precursory activity at volcanoes

steps.action: Collects published cases of declining precursors (Eyjafjallajökull 2010, Redoubt, Telica) and the gas-sealing explanation offered for stratovolcanoes.
steps.quote: some eruptions show a different behaviour, even a reduction in precursory activity immediately before eruption

steps.action: Uses earlier geodetic work, partly the authors' own, showing strain and stress accumulation along the Reykjanes plate boundary with a 5-8 km locking depth.
steps.quote: Geodetic measurements from the 1990s have shown strain and stress accumulation along the plate boundary

steps.action: Takes the live 24 February to 19 March 2021 unrest as the study window; the seismic network was densified with CAS/ÍSOR and Cambridge stations during the unrest (Methods).
steps.quote: Here we describe the activity from 24 February 2021, when the largest earthquake in the unrest episode occurred

steps.action: Records GNSS displacements (KRIV, LISK), 6-day Sentinel-1 interferograms and their LOS volumes (Fig. 2f), and seismicity rates, magnitudes and moment release; all decline towards the eruption onset.
steps.quote: which then gradually decreases to almost zero at the eruption onset

steps.action: Shows the deformation decline in independent data streams: GNSS, the descending InSAR track (Fig. 2) and the ascending track (Extended Data Fig. 2).
steps.quote: Also evident from InSAR is a decrease in deformation rate over time

steps.action: Relocates 1,321 small earthquakes with double differences and waveform cross-correlation in a better-fitting 1-D velocity model, mapping a two-segment vertical dyke and its migration over time.
steps.quote: reveal a vertical two-segment dyke, with a northern segment striking N45°E and a southern segment N25°E

steps.action: Uses pre-unrest InSAR strain (2015-2018) along the plate boundary axis, from the authors' earlier analysis, to justify including a plate-boundary shear source in the model.
steps.quote: Similar, but smaller, deformation was also present in the years preceding the unrest

steps.action: Inverts GNSS and two Sentinel-1 interferograms with Bayesian MCMC (GBIS) for a one-segment uniform dyke, a plate-boundary dislocation, two earthquake faults and a deflating point source.
steps.quote: An initial model considers a one-segment dyke with uniform opening and shearing

steps.action: Revises the source to a two-segment dyke with strikes fixed from the relocated seismicity and distributed opening on patches, with the plate boundary allowed shear only.
steps.quote: This model is then improved by considering a two-segment dyke, in line with relocated seismicity, with distributed opening and slip

steps.action: Solves daily incremental opening from GNSS by constrained least squares to obtain the daily magma inflow rate and the mean emplacement depth, which fall and shallow before the eruption.
steps.quote: and the lowest values (<10 m3 s−1) occur in the days before the eruption onset (15–19 March)

steps.action: Inverts synthetic GNSS data (constant volume rate, shallowing depth, added noise) to test whether the depth-volume trade-off creates the observed relation.
steps.quote: Despite the trade-off between depth and volume for individual days, the simulated constant volume change rate is retrieved, with no dependence on depth

steps.action: Fits a least-squares line between daily inflow rate and mean emplacement depth.
steps.quote: There appears to be a linear relationship between magma flow rate and mean depth of emplacement

steps.action: Proposes that the flow rate is controlled by flow up a conduit below the dyke, with no significant pressure needed to intrude along the dyke.
steps.quote: This is consistent with the flow rate being controlled by the flow up a conduit below the dyke

steps.action: Derives the laminar (Hagen-Poiseuille) conduit-flow relation between inflow rate and intrusion height, including the expression for conduit length.
steps.quote: Laminar flow of an incompressible fluid in the conduit is assumed

steps.action: Estimates a conduit length of 13 km (source depth about 19 km) and a radius of about 0.9 m from the fitted inflow rate and its gradient; notes the length does not depend on conduit shape.
steps.quote: gives L = 13 km, which puts the source depth at an estimated 19 km

steps.action: Compares the predicted initial eruption rate with photogrammetric observations, and the 19 km source depth with geochemical observations.
steps.quote: The correlation predicts an initial eruption rate of around 7 m3 s−1, in agreement with observations28

steps.action: Computes dilatational and Coulomb stress changes from the model sources (tens of MPa) and compares them with plate-loading rates (tens of kPa per year).
steps.quote: The estimated dilatational stress change at 3.5 km depth in the model is tens of megapascals

steps.action: Compares modelled simple shear with simple shear observed from ascending and descending InSAR at the plate-boundary axis.
steps.quote: illustrates well how the central axis of the plate boundary also plays an important role in releasing shear stress

steps.action: Forward-models deformation from 62 Mw ≥ 4 catalogue earthquakes with Coulomb software, compares the pattern with the inversion, and tests adding these faults to the inversion.
steps.quote: showing that the smaller earthquakes also contribute to stress release

steps.action: Keeps a three-stage account: dyke inflow with stress release, then declining inflow as emplacement shallows, then a quiet breach through weak upper crust.
steps.quote: a release of tectonic stress followed by a decline in deformation and seismicity rate may be a characteristic precursory activity

steps.action: Invokes the authors' earlier work (Krafla; buoyant magma bodies) on declining inflow expected from deep-source-to-shallow-body conduit flow.
steps.quote: An exponential decline in magma flow rate is expected in a magma conduit linking a deep source of constant pressure and a shallow magma body

steps.action: Compares the precursor pattern with published passive intrusions and rifting at Kilauea 1999, in East Africa, and at Tolbachik 1975-1976.
steps.quote: Precursory activity that we observe also resembles that observed before the 1975–1976 fissure eruption at Tolbachick volcano

steps.action: Extends the scope to rift eruptions fed into pre-stressed crust, with implications for Mauna Loa and observatory practice.
steps.quote: The precursory behaviour we observe may be relevant for eruptions in volcanic rifts in general

tree.answer: Deformation and seismicity decline in the days before the eruption
Rates are observed directly; dyke geometry, inflow rate, depth and stress are inferred
Explain the decline through dyke inflow and tectonic stress release
Escalation expectation (material failure forecast) and gas sealing are cited but not tested as rivals
No distinct predictions of rivals are computed
Conditions found in a live unrest and eruption

tree.question: 6b
tree.answer: Similar precursors at Kilauea, Tolbachik and in Afar are cited, not analysed
Synthetic inversion test, independent GNSS and InSAR data, eruption-rate and geochemical agreement, earthquake forward model
Staged stress-release model kept as an explanation
A peer-review file exists but was not supplied

end.claim: The 2021 Fagradalsfjall eruption was preceded by tectonic stress release during dyke emplacement, ending in a multi-day decline in deformation and seismicity as magma inflow fell and emplacement shallowed.

decisive_move.sentence: The daily inversion of GNSS data for dyke inflow rate and mean emplacement depth turns the observed decline into a declining, shallowing inflow, on which the conduit and stress-release account rests.

gates.evidence: Data come from routine observatory monitoring, densified to track the unrest, not from a stated hypothesis (§5.1 ¶1). The inversion method faced a synthetic test it could have failed (§5.4 ¶5), and the conduit model's eruption rate and source depth were checked against independent data (§3 ¶1). The staged account itself (§4 ¶1) is described as 'consistent with' the observations and faced no test against rivals. Nothing is reported as fixed before the data were seen.

imports.item: Markov-chain Monte Carlo with the Metropolis-Hastings algorithm

novelty_claims.quote: an unusually large number (64) of MW ≥ 4.0 earthquakes, nearly 20 more than recorded in the area during the whole two preceding decades
[...] activity, characterized by overlapping mainshock–aftershock sequences

limits: Only the published text and extended data were coded. The peer-review file is acknowledged (§A1.2 ¶1, PDF p. 10) but was not supplied, so no review sequence is coded. The paper does not say whether the one-segment-to-two-segment revision or the conduit model was prompted by review (inference: unknown). Rivals to the staged model (escalation, gas sealing) are cited but no rival predictions are computed. The gas-sealing explanation is set aside by noting that deformation also declined, not by a test. No MCMC convergence diagnostics are reported. Composition none_fits: this is a single live event with independent data streams and inversion checks, but there is no stated rival set (trace_series), no repeated cases (natures_repetition), and no new capability (capability_first). Sub-claims and their statuses: dyke volume of about 34 × 10^6 m3 and geometry (estimate_with_resolution, from posterior distributions); linear relation between flow rate and depth (regularity_in_range, within one event, with depths only where the volume rate exceeds 5 m3 s−1); conduit length 13 km, source depth 19 km and radius 0.9 m (estimate_with_resolution, but resting on assumed densities and viscosity, with no uncertainty propagated); stress release as a large fraction of 800 years of loading (best_explanation, order of magnitude); applicability to rift eruptions generally and to Mauna Loa (no status, a conjecture). The seismicity-rate analysis rests on automatic locations, with only 15-19% manually reviewed.

disagreements.target: Material failure forecast method (Voight 1988) and the expectation of escalating precursors
disagreements.support: Geodesy and seismicity at Fagradalsfjall show declining rather than escalating precursors, explained by tectonic stress release and shallowing emplacement.
disagreements.quote: This is a very different pattern of precursory activity from the case where activity escalates before eruptions as anticipated with the material failure forecast method

disagreements.target: Attribution of pre-eruptive seismic decline to sealing of gas pathways and pressurization (refs 15, 16)
disagreements.support: Here both seismicity and deformation declined, whereas sealing predicts uplift.
disagreements.quote: The precursory activity we observe at Fagradalsfjall, however, involves both a decline in seismicity and deformation.

disagreements.target: Standard SIL one-dimensional velocity model used in routine IMO locations
disagreements.support: The authors state the Reykjanes velocity structure differs from the SIL model and use a better-fitting model derived from body-wave and refraction data.
disagreements.quote: hypocentre depths, which tend to be roughly 1 km too deep in the routine analysis

alternatives_considered.chosen: Two-segment dyke with distributed opening and slip
alternatives_considered.alternatives: One-segment dyke with uniform opening and shearing
alternatives_considered.reason: In line with relocated seismicity; described as an improvement

alternatives_considered.chosen: Better-fitting local 1-D velocity model for relocation
alternatives_considered.reason: SIL depths tend to be roughly 1 km too deep on the Reykjanes Peninsula

alternatives_considered.chosen: Small events (0.5 < M < 1.4) for relative relocation
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Larger events including aftershocks on north-south faults
alternatives_considered.reason: To minimize contamination by aftershocks from strike-slip faults

alternatives_considered.chosen: Relocation excluding the stations closest to the dyke
alternatives_considered.reason: The method assumes waves from closely located events travel through the same velocity structure

alternatives_considered.chosen: Deflating point source for the subsidence near the eruption site
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Normal faulting related to the dyke intrusion

alternatives_considered.chosen: Shear-only plate-boundary dislocation in the final inversion
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Opening and shear on the plate-boundary dislocation
alternatives_considered.reason: Very little opening (9 cm) was assigned in the second inversion

alternatives_considered.chosen: Main inversion without the smaller earthquake faults
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Including the 62 smaller Mw ≥ 4 faults in the inversion
alternatives_considered.reason: Including them did not improve the fit to the geodetic data
Flow focuses into cylindrical paths; the length estimate is independent of the viscous term

alternatives_considered.chosen: Seismicity-rate analysis on automatic locations with M > 1
alternatives_considered.reason: Only a fraction of the seismicity was manually reviewed; completeness about M1 during the swarms
